content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper aims at solving the efficiency issue of the EOT attack, which targets at attacking models equipped with random mechanism.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strength
This paper studies an important and practical problem. I have not checked every detail, but the method seems reasonable to me.

## Weakness
The biggest problem is, as a research work that attempts to design an efficient attacking algorithm, the experimental results in this work is rather limited, and certainly does not reach the standard of a published work. Figure 2/3 do not offer too much information. And Table1/2 did not compare many concurrent methods or test on defensive models equipped with random mechanism.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a stochastic programming framework for attack methods against in-test dense with stochastic inference. Based on this framework, the paper proposes to accelerate the attack process with modern optimization techniques like momentum, adam and SVRG. Further the paper proposes to accelerate the attack process with pre-stored fixed randomness.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
* The paper is well-written.

Weaknesses:

I don't think the paper's contribution is enough for a top-tier conference like ICLR. 

The first half of the paper just introduces the existing works on stochastic inference. Although the authors state that they are the first to propose a stochastic programming framework for this kind of attack, I don't think this is a non-trivial contribution. 

For the second part the authors first proposed to use modern techniques like momentum, adam and SVRG to accelerate attack. Utilizing momentum, adam etc in PGD attack is a well-known technique and is used in many open-source attack codebases. For stochastic PGD, the only difference is that a batch is augmented by multiple randomized examples.

The authors further propose to use stored and fixed randomness to accelerate attack. But
1. How much time does this can save in attack? I think sampling the randomness is not a costly process. There is also no experiment on this.
2. The approach with fixed randomness is too straight-forward.

content.title: Efficient Stochastic Optimization for Attacking Randomness Involved Inference
content.abstract: Recent years witnessed a surging interest in test-time defense against adversarial attacks by introducing randomness during model inference. Notable examples include randomized smoothing equipped with probabilistic certified robustness and adversarial purification that leverages score-based generalization models. Specifically, the adversarial purification achieves state-of-the-art adversarial robustness under the strongest existing attack. Perhaps the most important component to developing and validating adversarial robustness is efficient attacks. Stochastic Projected Gradient Descent (S-PGD), which combines Expectation over Transformation (EOT) and PGD attacks, has become a common strategy to attack inference randomness and validate defense strategies. However, it often has severe efficiency issues that make it prohibitive for complete verification. For example, one step of S-PGD requires multiple runs of score-based purification models for each data point. This work revisits the techniques attacking randomness-involved inference and subsumes them into a unified stochastic optimization framework, which enables us to use acceleration and variance reduction techniques to largely improve the convergence and thus reduce the cost of attack. In other words, the proposed work can significantly improve attack performance, given a fixed budget for attacking.
